name: World Suicide Prevention Day: Creating Hope Through Action

content.title: World Suicide Prevention Day: Creating Hope Through Action
content.summary: Ending stigma begins with community-based campaigns that raise awareness and dispel misinformation about suicide

media.alt: World Suicide Prevention Day: Creating Hope Through Action

content.text: Suicide is a significant public health concern that can have long-term negative consequences for individuals, families, and communities. Over 700,000 people die by suicide every year, and it is the fourth largest cause of mortality among 15-19-year-olds, with low- and middle-income (LMIC) nations accounting for 77% of worldwide suicides.

Suicides are underreported due to the stigma associated with mental illness and seeking psychiatric assistance. Suicide prevention is undoubtedly a serious concern, particularly in LMIC, where a lack of finances, inadequate primary and mental health facilities, and weak political systems make preventative measures even more challenging. While current research in suicide prevention is mainly centred on high-income countries (HIC), preventive initiatives have been comparatively neglected in LMIC. Hence, World Suicide Prevention Day (WSPD) is an opportunity to change this and cultivate assistance in reducing preventable suicide deaths.

WSPD is a day to promote awareness and encourage mindfulness to those at risk of suicide and who are plagued by suicidal thoughts and actions. By eliminating discrimination and condemnation of people, we empower individuals with lived suicide experiences to share their stories and foster action to acquire resources for improving wellbeing while being a light of hope for people suffering from the condition.

Ending stigma begins with community-based campaigns that raise awareness and dispel misinformation about suicide. Unfortunately, the lack of understanding and persistent reliance on misinterpreted beliefs have impeded positive regard for individuals with lived suicide experiences. For example, the problematic perception that 'questioning suicidality is a trigger for suicidal inclinations. In actual fact, assessing for suicidality encourages people to disclose their suffering, reducing psychological distress and connecting them to mental health professionals and other resources.

Furthermore, suicide reporting, prevention, evaluation, and management trainings aid in aligning the needs of individuals with suicidal thoughts and actions with evidence-based care. Suicide support gaps have been identified among healthcare personnel, media practitioners, police, educational practitioners, clergy, and administrative leaders. On the other hand, training has been shown to enhance knowledge, alter negative attitudes, and improve abilities. In addition, they can be pivotal in decriminalising suicide and other legislative changes. As a result, training is a proper step in achieving the aim of our 2022 WSPD theme which is Creating Hope Through Action.

At BMI, we support healthcare workers' suicide assessment and management training needs. We are working with our implementation scientists and external partners to develop an interactive, practical, and informative module. The module will help healthcare workers build the necessary skills and competencies to promote mental wellness among people with lived suicide experiences. We hope to pilot-test the module among healthcare workers in AKU during the implementation of the Electronic Health Records system and later partner with health facilities in the region to implement the same.
Through raising awareness, encouraging people with suicide lived experiences to share their stories and supporting training, people can acquire the confidence to take action in suicide prevention.
What other actions/activities do you know of that can create hope among people with suicidal thoughts and action?
